title: Learning to Say No at Work
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] For nearly two years, I built a reputation as the colleague who never refused extra work, no matter how full my schedule already was.
Narrator: Whenever someone needed a report finished quickly, or a presentation rewritten overnight, they came straight to my desk, confident I would say yes.
Narrator: [carefully] I liked being seen as reliable, even though the constant extra tasks were slowly draining every ounce of energy I had left.
Narrator: Despite feeling exhausted most evenings, I kept accepting new requests, worried that refusing would make me look lazy or uncommitted.
Narrator: [reflective] Eventually I became ill and sought appropriate care, taking a week of leave. I do not claim workload alone diagnosed or caused the illness.
Narrator: During recovery, I recognized that hiding overload was not helping planning. Managers also had responsibility for staffing, priorities, and a safe workload.
Narrator: [honestly] So when I returned, I decided to change how I responded to requests, even though the idea genuinely terrified me at first.
Narrator: Instead of saying yes immediately, I started asking one simple question: if I take this on, what will I have to postpone?
Narrator: [seriously] That question changed everything, because it made the real cost of every yes completely visible, both to me and to whoever was asking.
Narrator: The first time I said no to my supervisor, my voice shook slightly, and I braced myself for disappointment or frustration.
Narrator: [gently] Instead, she simply nodded and said she hadn't realized how much I already had on my plate that particular week.
Narrator: Nobody had ever assumed I was overwhelmed, mainly because I had never once shown it clearly through my own words.
Narrator: [encouraging] Now I discuss priorities early and use appropriate support or accommodation channels when health or disability needs are relevant, without sharing unnecessary details.
Narrator: Ironically, since I started saying no occasionally, colleagues seem to trust my yes even more than they did before.
Narrator: [sincere] I suppose reliability was never about accepting everything. It was always about being honest concerning what I could actually manage well.

quiz.question: What reputation did the narrator build over nearly two years?
options: Someone who never refused extra work
quiz.explanation: He built a reputation as the colleague who never refused extra work.

quiz.question: What eventually forced the narrator to change?
options: He got seriously sick and needed a week away from work
quiz.explanation: He got sick, seriously enough that he needed a full week away from work.

quiz.question: What question did the narrator start asking himself before accepting new tasks?
options: If I take this on, what will I have to postpone?
quiz.explanation: He started asking what he would have to postpone if he took on a new task.

quiz.question: How did his supervisor react the first time he said no?
options: She nodded and said she hadn't realized how much he already had on his plate
quiz.explanation: She simply nodded and said she hadn't realized how much he already had on his plate that week.

quiz.question: What does the narrator conclude about reliability?
options: It means being honest about what he can actually manage well
quiz.explanation: He concludes reliability was always about being honest concerning what he could actually manage well.

quiz.question: Why is accepting every task not reliable?
options: Hidden overload makes deadlines and quality less predictable
quiz.explanation: Capacity information is necessary for planning.

quiz.question: What does the postponement question accomplish?
options: It makes priorities and trade-offs visible to the requester
quiz.explanation: The question turns a vague no into a planning decision.

quiz.question: Who also owns workload decisions?
options: Managers and the organization, not only the employee

quiz.question: What should happen if health is affected?
options: Seek appropriate care and use available workplace support or accommodation channels
Accept more work to prove commitment
quiz.explanation: Health needs are not solved only by saying no.

quiz.question: Why does the narrator’s “yes” become more trustworthy?
options: It reflects actual capacity rather than fear of refusal
